recall.define: Define release time, response time, jitter, worst-case execution time, period and deadline without the glossary and name the source for each.
recall.distinguish: Give the distinction and a numeric example for: latency versus response time; measured maximum versus worst-case execution time; period versus deadline; preemptive scheduler versus cooperative scheduler; tick versus tickless timing.
recall.apply: A sensor task with a 10 ms period misses its deadline once an hour. Using release time, response time, jitter, interrupt latency and measured maximum, state which measurement separates a scheduling cause from an interrupt-masking cause, why a day of measurements still does not establish a worst-case execution time, and which term names the quantity the watchdog actually bounds.

entries.definition: The instant at which a particular job becomes eligible for execution under the task model, distinct from the time it starts running. Record release jitter and the event-to-release delay separately when the external event and eligible instant differ. Response time uses the declared release reference.

authority.locator: Sections2–4, printed pp.47–49: requests, environment and response time

idiom: release latency is start minus release; response is finish minus release
entries.misconception: A job's release time is when it starts executing.

entries.definition: The elapsed time from a job's declared release to completion, including waiting and interference as well as its own execution. It differs from execution demand and start latency. Comparing a finite observed response with a deadline is not a proof of worst-case response over all admitted schedules.

authority.locator: Sections2–4, printed pp.47–49: requests, environment and response time

distinguish_from.distinction: Latency ends when the handler or task starts; response time ends when the required work is finished.

entries.definition: The variation of a timing quantity (release, start or completion) between successive jobs relative to the ideal periodic instants; it is a distribution, reported with its maximum and its source, not a single number.

authority.locator: C1.8.3 CYCCNT cycle counter and related timers — CYCCNT definition and profiling notes

entries.misconception: Jitter is noise that averages out.

entries.definition: An upper bound on the execution time of a code path over all inputs and hardware states, established by analysis or exhaustive argument; a measured maximum is a lower bound on it and never a substitute. Written WCET after its first use.

authority.locator: C1.8.3 CYCCNT cycle counter and related timers — CYCCNT definition and profiling notes

distinguish_from.distinction: The largest value seen in a campaign; it depends on the inputs exercised and says nothing about unobserved paths or cache states.

entries.misconception: Running the task for a day gives its WCET.

entries.definition: The largest value of a timing quantity observed in a recorded campaign, reported with its inputs, clock, build identity and uncertainty; evidence about that campaign only.
entries.misconception: A measured maximum with a safety margin is a bound.

entries.definition: The interval between successive nominal releases of a periodic task. It is distinct from execution time and deadline. Under a simple periodic model, utilization is execution demand divided by period; period alone cannot determine demand. Absolute-phase delay accounting avoids accumulating execution time into each nominal interval, but does not guarantee dispatch or completion at that instant.

authority.locator: Section3, printed p.48: assumptions A1–A5 and task parameters

entries.misconception: Calling delay(10) at the end of the loop gives a 10 ms period (it gives 10 ms plus the execution time).

entries.definition: The latest permitted completion instant for a job; an absolute deadline is a time point and a relative deadline is an interval from release. In the Liu–Layland model the next periodic request is the deadline; other task models need not equate period and deadline. A hard requirement demands the declared guarantee under its assumptions, rather than merely good average timing.

authority.locator: Sections2–4, printed pp.47–49: requests, environment and response time

entries.misconception: Meeting deadlines in testing proves schedulability.

entries.definition: A firmware organization that repeatedly runs activities from a main loop. Interrupt handlers and devices can still interact with its state. A response bound requires bounds for each reachable activity, polling interval, blocking call and interrupt interference; the presence of a loop alone supplies no bound. Polling and event handling policies must be stated.
entries.misconception: A superloop has no concurrency problems (interrupt handlers still share state with it).

entries.definition: A scheduler in which ordinary task switching depends on yield or blocking points. A single-core task cannot assume this removes all concurrent interference: interrupts, callbacks, additional cores and the execution-environment memory model still matter. A task that does not yield or block can delay another ready task indefinitely.

authority.locator: tasks.c configUSE_PREEMPTION macros, lines67–109; task.h taskYIELD

distinguish_from.distinction: A preemptive scheduler switches tasks on timer or interrupt events at arbitrary points, bounding response time but reintroducing shared-state hazards.

entries.misconception: Cooperative scheduling is always simpler and safer.

entries.definition: A scheduler that can replace a running task without that task voluntarily yielding, subject to interrupt masking, scheduler locking, priorities and port rules. Preemption creates possible interleavings; required synchronization depends on which state is actually shared and accessed, not merely on the existence of preemption.

authority.locator: tasks.c configUSE_PREEMPTION macros, lines67–109; task.h taskYIELD

entries.definition: Saving the running task's registers and stack pointer and restoring another task's, on Cortex-M split between the hardware exception frame and the software-saved callee registers in PendSV; its cost and its interaction with the floating-point context are measurable dispatch overheads.
entries.misconception: A context switch is free on a microcontroller.

entries.definition: A scheduler time-accounting event, often generated periodically by SysTick or another timer. Timer frequency, quantization, delayed servicing and coalesced pending state affect observed time; one interrupt does not prove that exactly one period elapsed. Tickless accounting must reconcile elapsed time and programmed wakeups. Timer resolution alone is not a bound on timeout completion latency.
entries.misconception: Timeouts are accurate to the tick period (they are accurate to within one tick plus jitter).

entries.definition: The return of a free-running counter to zero after its maximum; comparisons of absolute timestamps break at the wrap, while unsigned differences modulo the counter width remain correct as long as intervals are shorter than half the range.
entries.misconception: A 32-bit millisecond counter never wraps in practice (it wraps after about 49.7 days).

entries.definition: A monitoring timer that triggers a configured recovery action if its service contract is missed. STM32F4 IWDG requires service before timeout using its independent LSI clock; WWDG additionally detects a too-early refresh window. Timing depends on clock tolerance and debug configuration. Refresh should reflect verified application progress: an unconditional timer-handler refresh can conceal a stalled application, though refresh from an interrupt is not inherently invalid.

authority.locator: 21.1–21.4.1, pp.711–713: IWDG versus WWDG and debug mode

entries.misconception: Refreshing the watchdog from an interrupt proves the main loop is alive.

entries.definition: Deriving a stack-use bound from the reachable call graph, frame requirements, recursion limits, context saves and admissible interrupt nesting under a stated compiler/ABI model. A fill-pattern high-water observation measures bytes changed in the tested executions and cannot replace that argument. Dynamic or indirect calls and library/port frames must be accounted for explicitly.

authority.locator: tasks.c prvTaskCheckFreeStackSpace and uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark, lines6364–6455; task.h high-water API contract

entries.misconception: The high-water mark after a test run is the stack requirement.

entries.definition: A work check and sleep transition can miss a notification that is handled between them. Prevent it with a proven predicate/publication/wakeup protocol for the exact processor. On Armv7-M WFI wake eligibility ignores PRIMASK in its specified manner; WFE consumes event-register state and follows different rules. Recheck the predicate after wakeup and tolerate spurious or ignored hints. Interrupt masking alone is not a universal lost-wakeup repair.
